title: Solving Systems with Inverse Matrices
short: Write AX = B and multiply by A⁻¹ on the left.
trouble: Students multiply by A⁻¹ on the right, computing BA⁻¹.

blocks.html: A system of equations can be written as one matrix equation, $AX = B$. If $A$ has an inverse, you can solve it the way you solve $3x = 12$, as long as you respect the fact that matrix multiplication depends on order. It is an alternative to row reduction.

The system $ax + by = e$, $cx + dy = f$ is $$\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} e \\ f \end{bmatrix}, \text{ that is } AX = B.$$ If $A$ is invertible, multiply both sides on the left by $A^{-1}$: $X = A^{-1}B$.

$A^{-1}(AX) = (A^{-1}A)X = IX = X$, and the right side becomes $A^{-1}B$. The inverse must go on the left of both sides, because that is where it meets $A$. Putting it on the right would give $AXA^{-1}$, which does not simplify. Once you have $A^{-1}$, a new right side $B$ costs only one multiplication, which is why computers use this idea for many systems with the same coefficients.

blocks.title: A two-by-two system
blocks.q: Solve $3x + y = 7$, $5x + 2y = 12$ using an inverse matrix.

blocks.title: A given inverse
blocks.q: The coefficient matrix of a system has $A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & -1 \\ -2 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$, and the constants are $B = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}$. Find $(x, y, z)$.

blocks.title: A new right side
blocks.q: Using the same $A$ as in the first example, solve $3x + y = 1$, $5x + 2y = 3$.

blocks.html: Multiplying by $A^{-1}$ on the right and computing $BA^{-1}$. For a column $B$ that product is not even defined, and for square $B$ it usually gives the wrong matrix. Write the step out: $A^{-1}AX = A^{-1}B$. The inverse sits next to $A$, on the left.
